lines.text: Last time you drew a path in the editor and the robot followed it. This path has a single stop, and nobody draws it. You hold a button, and the robot goes there.
The target is a spot on the field, measured from the blue corner. The robot only gets there if it knows where it's standing right now, and wheels alone lose track.
A drawn path is only a list that gets read from a file, so the same list can be built in code. Here it has one entry.
Look at what's missing. There's no starting point anywhere, because the path begins wherever the robot happens to be when the command starts.
It comes out of the same builder as your drawn paths, so it gets the same controllers, the same speed limits, and the same idea of close enough.
The alliance flip comes along too. You write the goal for blue, and on red the same button drives to the matching spot on your own side of the field.
Two buttons, two spots. One brings the robot back to the field origin, and the other sends it a few meters away, turned to face the opposite direction.
Both are held, not tapped. Let go partway and the command is canceled, with a zero sent on the way out, so the robot stops where it is.
Once it arrives, the command is over. Your sticks have the drivetrain back, even with the button still down.
When you test it, don't skip the third step. Run the far spot on blue, switch to red, and run it again. The second time it should finish at the other end of the field, facing the other way.
That's why you look at the alliance before holding the button on a real robot. On a floor with no field, red puts the target a whole field length away, and the robot will try to get there.
Any spot you can write as a coordinate, the robot can now drive to. It's only as good as the pose it starts from, and the camera that keeps that honest comes next.
